title: Still LA's Best Biryani: The Little Bangladesh Strip-Mall Spot Worth The Drive
excerpt: Eater LA's Rebecca Roland reaffirms the verdict: the city's best biryani is still at Biriyani Kebob House in Little Bangladesh, where a former aeronautical engineer's kitchen turns out Hyderabadi lamb biryani that tastes like home.
body:
• Eater LA dining critic Rebecca Roland's latest Dining Report reaffirms it: the best biryani in Los Angeles is still at Biriyani Kebob House, 3525 W 3rd St, at the edge of Koreatown in Little Bangladesh.
  • Order the Hyderabadi lamb biriyani — aromatic basmati layered with a lamb shank the size of a football, served with tandoor-blistered naan. Beef nihari, chicken karahi, and seekh kabobs are the supporting cast worth the trip.
  • It's open daily, 11 am to 11 pm, everything halal, entrees mostly under $25. Counter-service casual: order at the counter, grab a table, don't forget to ask for more chutney. Parking is tight.
  • Opened in 2014 by former aeronautical engineer Enam Karim, the kitchen pulls from Pakistani, Bangladeshi, and North Indian traditions — a reminder that "Indian food" in LA is really a South Asian chorus.

A Strip-Mall Legend Holds Its Crown

Every few years, the debate over Los Angeles's best biryani reopens — and every few years, it ends at the same address. Eater LA's Rebecca Roland, the site's deputy editor for the Southern California/Southwest region, put it plainly in her recent Dining Report: Biriyani Kebob House, sitting at the crossroads of Koreatown and Little Bangladesh since 2014, is still serving warm naan blistered in a tandoor oven and the best biryani in Los Angeles. The verdict covers the fundamentals that matter: generous portions, warm family-style service, and a Hyderabadi lamb biriyani that outclasses flashier competition.

The Infatuation, which keeps the restaurant on its best Indian and Pakistani restaurants in LA list, describes the signature plate in a way that will be familiar to anyone who has ordered it: "an aromatic plate of basmati rice laced with spices that comes with lamb shank the size of a football." Curries perfumed with cardamom, turmeric, and ginger arrive with house-baked naan; beef nihari, seekh kabobs, and slow-cooked stews round out the table.

Context & Background

Biryani is not one dish but a family of them — Hyderabadi dum biryani layered and sealed for slow steaming, Kolkata's potato-and-egg version, Lucknow's Awadhi style, the Dhaka kacchi where meat and rice cook together from raw. What Biriyani Kebob House serves under the Hyderabadi banner leans into the kacchi technique: long, careful cooking where the meat and rice must finish together, demanding an almost obsessive attention to timing.

That fits the backstory. Founder Enam Karim is a former aeronautical engineer, and the precision shows — spices that pour out of the rice when the plate arrives, meat that doesn't need cutting. As the restaurant's own description puts it, it is an Indian, Pakistani, and Bangladeshi restaurant: a deliberate fusion in a neighborhood — Little Bangladesh — that has been a centre of Bangladeshi life in LA since the 1960s. Walk a few blocks and the whole street becomes a food argument in the best way: Aladin Sweets for tehari and roshogolla, Roshona Bilash for Bengali-style biryani and fuchka.

Impact & Analysis

Why does a no-frills strip-mall counter keep winning? Partly economics: when entrees sit under $25 and portions arrive generously, the value equation is hard to beat. But the deeper reason is culinary honesty. Biryani is easy to fake — spiced rice and meat called biryani by name only — and much of LA's Indian food scene leans toward polished, pan-Indian menus built for a broad audience. This kitchen cooks the way a family does: one region's technique, done properly, every day.

The takeaway for the diaspora is cultural as much as culinary. Reviews from regulars keep landing on the same note: it tastes like home, whichever home you came from. The menu's cross-border logic — Pakistani karahi, Bangladeshi kachey lamb biriyani, North Indian tandoori — mirrors how many diaspora families actually eat, at tables where Punjabi, Hyderabadi, and Bengali dishes share the same spread.

Diaspora Angle

For Indian Angelenos, this is the kind of place that becomes a fixed point — the Friday biryani run, the dinner that converts visitors. In a city where South Asian dining increasingly splits between upscale reimaginings downtown and Santa Monica and the humble neighborhood spots of the San Fernando Valley, Biriyani Kebob House is proof the latter still sets the standard. Its all-halal menu also makes it a gathering table for Muslim and mixed-community families across the city.

What's Next

LA's South Asian food map keeps expanding — a recent 2026 dining guide from Tadka Table names Roshona Bilash, Aladin Sweets, and Pijja Palace among the rooms to try, evidence that Little Bangladesh and its surroundings are having a moment. The best move: eat the biryani at 3rd Street first, then let the neighborhood's Bengali kitchens argue with your palate for second and third rounds.
